title: Delayed Momentum Aggregation: Communication-efficient Byzantine-robust Federated Learning with Partial Participation
claim: Under heavy attack and low participation, baselines collapse or plateau while the proposed method stays stable and reaches the best accuracy.
layout: 2 stacked blocks of 2x5 line-plot grids, shared legend, captions per block
description: Two stacked blocks, (a) and (b), each a 2x5 grid of small line plots of test accuracy against epoch. Top rows are IID data and bottom rows are non-IID data. Columns are five attacks: ALIE, BF, IPM, LF and Mimic, all under CCLIP aggregation. Four colored curves with shaded variance bands appear in each plot: FedAvg (red), FedCM (orange), DeMoA (purple, labeled as the proposed method) and Byz-VR-MARINA-PP (dark navy). Block (a) is MNIST with p=0.5. There the FedAvg and FedCM curves stop at epoch 3, which marks their collapse. Block (b) is CIFAR-10 with p=0.1 over 1000 epochs. There only DeMoA and Byz-VR-MARINA-PP survive. DeMoA is clearly higher in the non-IID panels. A shared legend sits under each block. The eye goes first to the purple curves and the truncated baselines.
caption: Byzantine-robust training with Byzantine ratio $\delta=0.2$ using centered clipping (CCLIP). Top: IID data; bottom: non-IID data; columns correspond to different attacks. \algname{FedAvg} and \algname{FedCM} eventually encounter a Byzantine majority round and collapse, while \algname{Byz-VR-MARINA-PP} remains stable but attains lower test accuracy than \algname{DeMoA} due to their bias from clipping.
abstract: Partial participation is essential for communication-efficient federated learning at scale, yet existing Byzantine-robust methods typically assume full client participation. In the partial participation setting, a majority of the sampled clients may be Byzantine, once Byzantine clients dominate, existing methods break down immediately. We introduce delayed momentum aggregation, a principle where the central server aggregates cached momentum from non-sampled clients along with fresh momentum from sampled clients. This principle ensures Byzantine clients remain a minority from the server's perspective even when they dominate the sampled set. We instantiate this principle in our optimizer DeMoA. We analyze the convergence rate of DeMoA, showing that DeMoA is Byzantine-robust under partial participation. Experiments show that, with 20% Byzantine ratio and only 10% partial participation rate, DeMoA achieves the best accuracy even when existing methods fail empirically.
